cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal:
Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random for the fair-coin product measure? In the precise model below, determine whether
\[\forall X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad
\operatorname{KLR}(X)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{MLR}(X).\]
The reverse implication is known, so this is equivalently equality of the two randomness classes. Betting strategies may choose fresh coordinates adaptively, need not visit every coordinate, and are ordinary partial computable procedures without an oracle.
cards.definitions:
Space and measure. Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) consists of all functions \(X:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), including noncomputable ones. Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) be the finite binary strings. For a string \(\sigma\), its length is \(|\sigma|\), and its cylinder is
\[[\sigma]=\{X:\ X(i)=\sigma(i)\text{ for all }i<|\sigma|\}.\]
The fair-coin product probability measure \(\mu\) makes coordinates independent and assigns \(\mu([\sigma])=2^{-|\sigma|}\). No bias, alternative measure or oracle relativization is involved.

Martin-Löf tests. A uniformly effectively open family is specified by one ordinary Turing program enumerating a set \(W\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\times2^{<\mathbb N}\). Put
\[U_k=\bigcup_{(k,\sigma)\in W}[\sigma].\]
It is a Martin-Löf test when \(\mu(U_k)\le2^{-k}\) for every \(k\ge1\). This condition concerns the measure of the union, not the sum of cylinder measures when cylinders overlap. Repetitions in an enumeration are harmless, no disjointness or prefix-free presentation is required, and levels need not be nested. The measure bound is a mathematical condition on a test; the enumerating program is not required to certify it or compute the exact measure. Define
\[\operatorname{MLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{for every Martin-Löf test }(U_k)_{k\ge1},\quad X\notin\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k.\]
Uniform enumeration across all levels is mandatory.

Histories and betting procedures. A history is a finite ordered list
\[h=((j_0,a_0),\ldots,(j_{s-1},a_{s-1}))\]
with distinct \(j_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\). It records precisely the coordinates already queried and their observed values, in query order. A strategy is a deterministic partial computable function \(S\) which, on such a history, either fails to return an action or returns
\[S(h)=(j,q),\qquad j\notin\{j_0,\ldots,j_{s-1}\},\quad q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,2].\]
Every returned action on a valid history must meet these conditions. Computability means a finite Turing-machine program operating on an effective finite encoding of this list, natural coordinates, and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs. These encodings carry no resource bound. The program receives only the history; it cannot inspect any further bit of \(X\) before choosing its action, use an oracle, or use an uncomputable real parameter. Internal deterministic work and previously computed data can be recovered from the history and program. The equivalent history of observed bit values alone suffices when the query coordinates are reconstructed by rerunning that same strategy.

Run and capital. Start at empty history with capital \(C_0^S(X)=1\). If \(S(h_s)=(j_s,q_s)\) returns, reveal \(a_s=X(j_s)\), append \((j_s,a_s)\), and update
\[C_{s+1}^S(X)=\begin{cases}
C_s^S(X)q_s,&a_s=0,\\
C_s^S(X)(2-q_s),&a_s=1.
\end{cases}\]
The two possible multipliers average to one, so the bet is fair on a fresh unbiased bit. Capital is always nonnegative, with no borrowing or outside deposits; zero capital remains zero. The choice \(q_s=1\) reads a bit without risking capital. Coordinates may be arbitrarily large and need not increase. They cannot repeat, including after a zero wager. There is no requirement to query every coordinate even on an infinite run.

If the next computation diverges or returns no action, the run has no further completed bets and earns no further capital. Computation time itself does not increase capital. There are no time or space bounds. Let \(D_S(X)\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the finite or infinite initial segment of completed-bet counts, including zero. The strategy succeeds precisely when
\[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)>K.\]
This is unbounded supremum of capital, not a requirement that capital converge to infinity, grow at a computable rate, or exceed a single fixed threshold.

Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness. Let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of all strategies just specified. Define
\[\operatorname{KLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The bound may depend on both \(S\) and \(X\), and no algorithm producing those bounds is required. Rational stakes and unit initial capital give the standard notion. Replacing partial computability by total computability gives the same randomness class, but requiring every coordinate to be visited is a separate condition and is not imposed here.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its negation, with these exact measure, effectiveness and betting conventions.

A positive answer must hold for every infinite binary sequence and every uniformly effective Martin-Löf test. Equivalently, prove that for each \(X\) failing some Martin-Löf test there exists an admissible computable strategy with unbounded capital on \(X\). That existential strategy may depend on \(X\); it must still be a finite oracle-free program. A uniform conversion of tests to a finite universal family of strategies is not an additional requirement.

A negative answer must prove the existence of one sequence \(X\) and one Martin-Löf test \((U_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that
\[X\in\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\ C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The same sequence must satisfy every test level and defeat every allowed strategy. A nonconstructive existence proof qualifies; an algorithm computing the bits of \(X\) is not required. Different sequences for different levels or strategies, a separation for fixed query orders, a generalized betting game, or a frequency-only stochasticity result does not settle the full target. Finite simulations or a one-sided known implication are insufficient.
cards.why: Determines whether adaptive computable fair betting detects every effective measure-theoretic failure of randomness in an individual infinite sequence. Equality or separation would connect two foundational ways to formalize unpredictability.

importance.reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.

progress.text: Merkle and coauthors establish computable splitting and high-density subsequence results for Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences.
Kastermans–Lempp separate predetermined permutation and injective query-order randomness from Martin-Löf randomness.
Franklin–Porter retain the equality question in their historical survey and state the partial/total convention.
Petrović’s universal pair applies to generalized half-betting strategies.
The open-set-game preprint establishes a quantitative obstruction, without a separating infinite sequence.
The open-set result appears in Theoretical Computer Science and retains the equality problem.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 primary paper and journal record retain KLR=MLR as open. Its open-set result concerns level-dependent witnesses and is not a separating sequence. Restricted query orders, generalized partitions and pairwise nonuniversality results do not settle the full stated class. No matching resolution was found in the bounded later-work search; complete cited proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: Martin-Löf randomness and betting randomness concern individual infinite objects. Effective tests describe events of arbitrarily small fair-coin probability, while a gambler uses observed bits to determine future bets. Neither definition is a confidence score for a finite sample. Every finite binary string can occur at the start of a Martin-Löf random sequence, so a finite unusual-looking prefix alone cannot settle membership in either class.

Adaptivity changes the information available to a strategy. It may inspect coordinate 100, then choose between coordinates 3 and 7 based on that value. Reading a bit with no money at risk still reveals it and makes it unavailable for later betting. The strategy must choose its next fresh position and wager using only its current history; otherwise it could exploit information it has not legitimately obtained.

The established implications are \(\operatorname{MLR}\subseteq\operatorname{KLR}\subseteq\operatorname{CR}\), where computable randomness \(\operatorname{CR}\) rules out successful total computable fair gamblers that read bits in their original order. The first inclusion is the known direction; the card asks whether it is equality. Kolmogorov–Loveland stochasticity instead controls limiting frequencies of adaptively selected bits and is a different, weaker requirement than defeating all fair betting strategies.

Partiality must be separated from which bits are eventually visited. The standard theory permits partial computations, and using total nonmonotonic procedures yields the same randomness class. However, a total procedure can still leave infinitely many coordinates unseen. Requiring a total strategy to visit every coordinate changes its power: the classical source shows that such a strategy can be matched by a monotonic gambler on every sequence where it succeeds.

Kastermans and Lempp separate Martin-Löf randomness from randomness against predetermined computable permutation orders, and against the more general predetermined computable injective orders. A permutation visits every position; an injection may omit positions. In both cases the query order is fixed independently of revealed bit values. These separations therefore do not decide what fully adaptive strategies can detect.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan show that a Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequence has Martin-Löf random subsequences on computable sets of coordinates with densities arbitrarily close to one. Their Theorem 12 says that splitting at any infinite co-infinite computable set leaves at least one Martin-Löf random part. These are substantial proximity results, but randomness of a subsequence does not establish randomness of the whole interleaving.

Petrović’s universal-pair result concerns a generalized half-betting game. Such games allow richer computable partitions of the remaining possible sequences than asking for the value of one fresh coordinate. A pair of generalized strategies can cover all failures of Martin-Löf randomness, but this theorem does not turn them into strategies in the more restricted query model of the card.

The 2025 open-set theorem is stronger than merely a statement about one finite family: it assigns bounds to all Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies and finds arbitrarily small effective open sets, each containing a sequence staying below every strategy’s bound. The witnessing sequence can depend on the open-set level. The result does not give one such sequence in every level of a single Martin-Löf test, and the paper leaves equality open.

The decisive quantifiers concern one infinite sequence at a time. For a negative answer, that sequence must fail an effective test and simultaneously evade every permitted computable gambler. For a positive answer, a successful gambler may be different for different nonrandom sequences. The mathematical question does not require one fixed gambler, a fixed finite family, or uniform speed of winning.

sentences: Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies make computable fair bets while adaptively querying previously unseen coordinates of an infinite binary sequence.
The problem asks whether defeating every such strategy implies passing every uniform effective null test for fair-coin measure.
Strategies may be partial and may omit coordinates forever, but they cannot borrow, revisit observed bits or inspect them through an oracle.
A complete Lean answer must prove the implication or exhibit one non-Martin-Löf-random sequence on which every strategy has bounded capital.
Known subsequence theorems, nonadaptive-order separations and the 2025 open-set obstruction leave that exact comparison unresolved.

source_formulation.text: Preserves importance 96 and the inherited fair-coin KLR⇒MLR question, rather than replacing it with a finite-family uniformity assertion from the source’s open-set game. The operational rational multiplier formulation is the standard scan-rule/stake-function model of Merkle and coauthors and Kastermans–Lempp. The review specifies partial computations and explicitly permits permanent omission of coordinates; neither computational resource bounds nor oracle access is added.

Checked the partial/total convention; it does not impose exhaustive scanning.

Read full Kastermans–Lempp author PDF §1.1, pp.4–6: scan/stake functions, fairness, unbounded success and rational-valued formulation; §§2–3 cover nonadaptive permutation/injective separations. The publisher identifies TCS411(3),602–616,6 January2010.

Read Franklin–Porter arXiv:2004.02851 §4.4, Definition 4.32 and adjacent discussion: standard implication directions, partial/total equivalence and open equality. This also verifies the inherited textbook-note scope.

Read Petrović arXiv:2403.19817v2 full introduction, Definition 2.2, Theorem 1 and game definitions/Lemma 3.2. The countable-family obstruction has witnesses depending on the level. Checked journal metadata and the upload/title-page date distinction; did not independently certify the full proof.

Checked the 2021 generalized half-betting publisher abstract and its discussion in the full 2025 primary source; full 2021 proof not inspected. Also screened arXiv:2212.14279 abstract: nonuniversality of pairs under scanning restrictions does not separate the full classes.

Bounded arXiv/publisher searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching later resolution. Third-party auto-summaries that claim the 2025 paper separates the classes conflict with its primary statement and were not used. Checked logical negation and finite-prefix examples mathematically; no Lean proof has been produced.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
